# Education in Finland
Education in Finland is deeply rooted in its history, linked to Lutheranism’s emphasis on literacy since the 16th century. The modern system evolved from early Swedish-language schooling to Finnish-language universal education, with compulsory basic comprehensive education (grades 1–9) established in the 1970s. Since September 2021, upper secondary education (academic lukio or vocational school) is also compulsory until age 18, with no "gifted" programs; instead, collaboration and peer support are emphasized. Early childhood education, not mandatory but widely utilized, focuses on play-based learning that fosters independence, social skills, and respect for individuality from birth to age 7. Free universal daycare and preschool prepare children for formal schooling, embedding a culture of reading and lifelong learning.
The Finnish education system is municipally funded and administered, largely free of tuition or fees, including for private (mostly faith-based or Waldorf) schools. Small class sizes (around 20 students), autonomy for teachers with master's degrees, bilingualism (Finnish and Swedish), emphasis on arts, crafts, and outdoor activities, comprehensive social support (free meals, healthcare, materials), and minimal formal homework characterize the basic education experience. Upper secondary schooling spans three to four years with vocational and academic tracks, free tuition, health care, and meals. Graduation certificates are awarded after matriculation exams for academic students and vocational certifications for vocational students. Tertiary education divides into research universities and universities of applied sciences, both merit-based with transparent admissions and mostly free for EU/EEA students. Adult education includes lifelong learning offerings such as “Open University” and free education institutes promoting broad personal development. Finland has also exported its educational expertise internationally through official schools abroad, Finnish-inspired private schools, and programs like Education Finland, underpinning its reputation as a global leader in education.
